name: libbi
desc: Bayesian state-space modelling on parallel computer hardware
why: Bayesian state-space modelling that runs on parallel hardware is real science you could run at home over a long weekend.

brief.what_it_is: LibBi is a toolkit for state-space modelling and Bayesian inference on parallel hardware, per its homepage and README. Its main pieces are a C++ template library and a parser and compiler, written in Perl, for LibBi's own modelling language, which is used to specify models. The staple methods are sequential Monte Carlo (particle filtering), including particle MCMC and SMC^2, with an extended Kalman filter and some parameter optimisation routines as other options. The sources I read do not say what output format inference produces.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage says LibBi is used for state-space modelling and Bayesian inference on high-performance computer hardware, including multi-core CPUs, many-core GPUs and distributed-memory clusters.
brief.how_it_works: Models are written in LibBi's own domain-specific language, and a Perl parser and compiler processes them into code built on the C++ template library. The README does not go further into the mechanism.
brief.install_notes: The README points to an INSTALL.md file, which I did not fetch, so I have no build steps. The homepage has a 'Download Stable' button and a news item from 14 Nov 2016 titled 'Easily install LibBi from Homebrew'. A 2014 news item says LibBi runs on Windows and Mac OS X. The brew metadata lists executables 'bi' and 'libbi', but I did not confirm these in the README. The getting-started and documentation pages I tried returned 404, so hardware, runtime and first-run requirements are unknown from my sources.
brief.standout: It is a Bayesian state-space toolkit built around particle-filter methods that targets GPUs and clusters, not only a single CPU. Its modelling language is compiled into a C++ template library, which is an unusual pairing. An R interface, RBi, is mentioned in the news.
brief.status: Quiet. The most recent release on the homepage news list is LibBi 1.4.5 on 08 Jul 2019, and the last item of any kind is dated 2019. I could not see a last-commit date from the GitHub README fetch, so this is based on the homepage news only.
brief.caveats: The homepage's 404 pages mean the docs and getting-started guide were unreachable, so the sources I read are thin on how to use it. Hardware needs, licence, and whether the Homebrew formula is current are not stated in what I read. The scout note's claim that this can be run at home over a long weekend is not supported by anything I fetched.

judge.reason: Its own modelling language and particle-filter methods make Bayesian state-space inference run across GPUs and clusters—a distinctive scientific rabbit hole, not generic plumbing.

entry.title: LibBi
entry.tldr: A modelling language and compiler for Bayesian state-space models, built around particle filters that can run on multi-core CPUs, GPUs and clusters.
entry.deeper_look:
LibBi is a toolkit for state-space modelling and Bayesian inference. You describe a system that changes over time, with hidden state you cannot observe directly and noisy measurements you can. LibBi then estimates the hidden state and the model's parameters from the data.

Models are written in LibBi's own domain-specific language. A parser and compiler written in Perl turn that description into code built on a C++ template library. In the project's words, "LibBi consists of a C++ template library, as well as a parser and compiler, written in Perl, for its own modelling language."

The staple methods are sequential Monte Carlo, also called particle filtering, including particle MCMC and SMC^2. An extended Kalman filter and some parameter optimisation routines are also on offer. The homepage says it targets "multi-core CPUs, many-core GPUs (graphics processing units) and distributed-memory clusters".

The idea underneath is that particle filters keep many guesses about the hidden state alive at once and reweight them as data arrives. That makes them a natural fit for parallel hardware. It is a door into probabilistic inference, tracking and time-series modelling from the angle of generated, parallel code. An R interface, RBi, is mentioned in the project news.
entry.install:
brew install libbi
# Homebrew pulls in autoconf, automake, boost, gsl, netcdf and qrupdate. The README points to an INSTALL.md for build details; GPU or cluster use likely needs extra setup that the sources do not describe.

Shows the help for the bi executable, the second command the formula installs.

entry.whats_unique: It pairs a small modelling language with a compiler that generates C++ template code, aimed at particle-filter methods on GPUs and clusters rather than a single CPU.
entry.caveats: The project has been quiet since the 1.4.5 release in July 2019, and the getting-started and documentation pages returned 404 when checked, so learning it means digging through the repository.
